teaser.en: The cashew grows its nut on the outside, hanging beneath a juicy 'apple' that most harvesters simply leave on the ground.

summary.en: *M'bibo* is the cashew tree, the premier cash crop of Kwale homesteads and farms. Its nuts bring income to thousands of families, and the Digo language has a whole vocabulary for its fruit.

about.en:
*M'bibo* is a spreading evergreen tree with large, leathery, rounded leaves and a low, wide crown. Its small pinkish flowers grow in loose clusters at the branch tips.

The fruit is unusual. What looks like the fruit is a swollen fleshy stalk, the cashew apple or *bibo*, red or yellow when ripe and full of astringent juice. The true fruit, the kidney-shaped nut (*ngorosho*), hangs from its lower end. Green, unripe apples are called *dunje*.

where.en: Cashew is one of the commonest trees of Kwale homesteads and farms, often planted in rows or scattered among coconuts and mangoes. It is easiest to notice in the harvest season, when the coloured apples hang among the leaves and drop to the ground.

uses.en:
The nuts are the money crop, sold for cash and processed for export and local markets. The shell around the kernel contains a caustic oil that burns the skin, so the nuts are roasted before they are cracked open to free the kernel. The shell oil itself is used as a varnish, and the tree also yields a gum.

The apples are eaten fresh or fermented into a drink, though at harvest many are simply left on the ground.

culture.en: Digo has words for every stage of the cashew. To crack the nuts open is *papata*, and an over-dried nut is *mkpwetse* or *mkeye*. A Mgombato example sentence captures the harvest: *Wakati wa kuendza ngorosho atu nkutsola ngorosho akaricha mabibo*, 'When gathering cashew nuts, people pick up the nut and leave the *bibo*.' The tree was brought to East Africa from Brazil by Portuguese traders centuries ago, and its names *m'bibo* and *mkorosho* are now used by all Digo.

names.en: Digo: *m'bibo* (also written *mbibo* or *mbibu*) for the tree, *ngorosho* for the nut, *bibo* for the apple and *dunje* for the unripe apple. *Mkorosho* is also used. Swahili: *mkorosho* or *mkanju*, with the nut called *korosho*. Giriama: *mkanju*. English: cashew. Scientists call it *Anacardium occidentale*.

reason.en: Mango, in the same family and also a cash crop

definition.en: The fleshy cashew apple, with the nut growing at its end. Mgombato: when gathering cashew nuts people pick up the nut and leave the apples.
The cashew fruit while it is green and unripe. Pakia notes that unripe cashew gives off a caustic sap, maronvi.
A cashew nut that has dried out too much.
A cashew nut that has dried out too much; the word also means an old, wizened person.
The cotyledons (seed leaves) of the cashew, which rise above the ground when the nut germinates. The Digo see their role as protecting the embryo.
A caustic, toxic oil from unripe cashew (dunje) and from the shell of mature nuts. Digo children learn early to avoid touching it.
A sticky resin from the bark of the cashew tree.

use.en: Used to glue things to a surface.

mgombato: bibo (ma) cashew fruit, at the end of which the cashew nut grows; kanju. Wakati wa kuendza ngorosho atu nkutsola ngorosho akaricha mabibo. When gathering cashewnuts people pick up the nut and leave the "bibo". (See: dunje, m'bibo, ngorosho)
dunje (ma) cashew fruit in green, unripe stage; dunge. (See: bibo)
m'bibo (mi) cashewnut tree (Anacardium occidentale); mkorosho, mkanju, mbibo. (See: bibo, ngorosho)
